teaser: An 80-year-old fortune-teller's river journey, saved from a dying man's fire.
review_notes:
IMAGE IS EXTREMELY PANORAMIC (1280 x 44 px): it shows the whole Master Wuyong scroll with its colophons as a thin strip. Only one interactive block, pointing at four broad stretches; no small details could be placed.
The painting occupies roughly x 0.38 to 0.98 of the image; everything left of 0.37 is colophon writing. Please confirm on a larger image.
The block of writing in the sky near the right end (x about 0.88) is believed to be the note added at the Qianlong court (written by Liang Shizheng) declaring this scroll a copy; the lesson only calls it later writing.
Columns just left of the last peak assumed to be Huang's own 1350 inscription.
Biography: clerk, jailed about 1315 in a tax scandal involving his superior, later Daoist and fortune-teller. Age about 80 by Western count in 1350.
Burning in 1650 by Wu Hongyu; rescue by his nephew; Remaining Mountain piece about 51 cm in Zhejiang Provincial Museum; Wuyong scroll about 33 x 637 cm.
Qianlong acquired the copy (Ziming scroll) in 1745 and the original in 1746; he inscribed the copy more than fifty times.
Reunion exhibition in Taipei, June 2011.

lesson.text: In 1350 Huang Gongwang was about eighty years old and owned very little. He had no post, no pension and no fixed address. He wandered the river towns south of the Yangzi as a Daoist priest, and when he needed money he told fortunes in the street.

It had not been the plan. As a young man he worked as a legal clerk in the government of the Mongol rulers of China. Around 1315 his superior was caught up in a tax scandal, and Huang went to prison with him. He came out with his career finished, turned to religion, and only then, near fifty, took up painting seriously.

By that year, 1350, a roll of paper had been riding in his luggage for more than three years. He had begun it at a retreat in the Fuchun hills, for a fellow Daoist known as Master Wuyong. He added to it only when the mood came, between journeys. That year he finally wrote a note on it, and the note explains why.

His friend was afraid that someone would grab the painting, “by trickery or by force,” before it was ever handed over. So Huang wrote on the unfinished scroll that it belonged to Wuyong. It was a receipt issued before delivery.

What you have on screen looks like a ribbon, and that is accurate. The surviving scroll is about 33 centimeters high and more than 6 meters long (roughly 13 inches by 21 feet). Nobody was meant to see it all at once. You unrolled it from the right, a shoulder's width at a time, and the river went by like a view from a boat.

lesson.title: Downriver, right to left
lesson.text: The ink landscape fills only the right-hand part of this strip. Start at the far right and drift left, as a reader of the scroll would.

spots.title: Setting out
spots.text: Low banks and clumps of trees, close to the water. A block of small writing, added by a later hand, floats in the sky. The journey starts quietly.

spots.title: The high country
spots.text: The hills pile up into peak after peak, some sharp, some rounded, with dark dots of trees along the ridges. This is the busiest, densest stretch of the whole river.

spots.title: Open water
spots.text: The mountains fall away. A few tall pines stand on a spit of land, and then there is almost nothing: bare paper for the river, a thin gray shore far off. The scroll breathes out.

spots.title: The last peak
spots.text: One final mountain rises alone at the left end of the painting, and the land stops. Just beyond it stand columns of writing: the journey is over and the words begin.

lesson.text: The painting is paced like music: a soft opening, a crowded middle, a long silence, one last chord. Huang composed time as much as space.

Seen at full size, the mountains are made of long, loose, slightly wavy lines laid side by side, like strands pulled from a rope. Chinese painters call them hemp-fiber strokes. Huang dragged a fairly dry brush over paper, went back over passages days or months later, and left his changes of mind visible.

That was the new thing. Earlier landscapes aimed to convince you a mountain was there. This one lets you watch a hand thinking. For the scholar-painters who came after, artists who painted for themselves and their friends rather than for pay, it became the model of what a picture should be: a record of a person, written in brushstrokes.

Three hundred years later the scroll belonged to a collector named Wu Hongyu, who loved it so much that on his deathbed, in 1650, he ordered it burned so it could go with him. A nephew pulled it out of the flames.

The fire had already eaten through the opening section. The scroll was cut at the scorched part and remounted as two paintings. The short first piece, about half a meter long, is called The Remaining Mountain and lives in Hangzhou. The long piece, the one in this image, went on to Taipei.

Now look at the left third of the strip, which holds no landscape at all. Those dense blocks are colophons, comments written by owners and admirers and mounted after the painting. On this scroll the writing runs on for meters: the paper trail of everyone who was moved by it.

In the 1740s the Qianlong Emperor acquired two versions, one year apart. He decided the copy was the real thing and covered it with more than fifty admiring inscriptions. The genuine scroll, dismissed as a fake, was left almost untouched.

An emperor's mistake turned out to be the painting's second rescue. And in 2011 the two burned halves were shown side by side in Taipei, together for the first time in three and a half centuries. Huang never knew any of it. He died in 1354, four years after writing his note, still, as far as anyone can tell, a wandering old man with ink in his bag.

quiz.question: How did Huang Gongwang earn money in his old age?
quiz.explanation: After prison ended his clerk's career he lived as a Daoist priest and fortune-teller.

quiz.question: Why did Huang write a note on the scroll in 1350 before it was finished?
options: To record that it belonged to Master Wuyong
To apologize for its poor quality
To offer it to the emperor
quiz.explanation: His friend feared someone would seize it, so Huang put the ownership in writing.

quiz.question: In which direction is the scroll read?
quiz.explanation: A handscroll is unrolled from the right, a section at a time.

quiz.question: Why is the painting in two pieces today?
options: Two heirs divided it by agreement
It was damaged in a fire ordered by a dying owner
Huang painted it on two separate sheets
quiz.explanation: Wu Hongyu had it thrown in the fire in 1650; the burned part was cut away and the halves remounted.

quiz.question: What are hemp-fiber strokes?
options: Long, loose, wavy lines laid side by side to build up hills
The texture of the paper itself
quiz.explanation: They look like strands pulled from a rope and give Huang's mountains their soft structure.

facts.text: The Qianlong Emperor wrote dozens of inscriptions on the genuine scroll.
facts.explanation: He lavished them on a copy he believed was authentic and left the real one almost untouched.

facts.text: The surviving long section of the scroll is more than 6 meters long.
facts.explanation: It is about 33 centimeters high and over 6 meters long.

facts.text: Huang Gongwang took up painting seriously only when he was close to fifty.
facts.explanation: He turned to painting after prison had ended his career as a clerk.
